previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, ICD placement, diabetes, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease was admitted for acute on chronic shortness of breath and orthopnea. The symptoms were attributed to an exacerbation of congestive heart failure, supported by elevated BNP, bibasilar crackles, and radiographic evidence of mild pulmonary edema. He was treated with intravenous furosemide and supplemental oxygen, with improvement in symptoms and a reduction in weight to his dry weight of 176 pounds. His renal function, initially impaired with a creatinine of 1.6, improved to 1.4 by discharge. Lisinopril was not restarted due to residual orthostatic hypotension and elevated creatinine. His diabetes was managed with insulin during admission, and Januvia was resumed at discharge. He experienced non-sustained ventricular tachycardia on telemetry but remained stable. He was discharged home with instructions on weight monitoring, fluid and sodium restriction, and follow-up with cardiology and primary care.

Brief Hospital Course:
Mr. ___ is a ___ yo M with PMHX of nonischemic CM EF 
___, VT s/p AICD, DM2, HTN, CKD who presented with dyspnea on 
exertion and fatigue x 1 day. His symptoms resolved on 
presentation to floor. Etiology remained uncertain, and may have 
been a combination of mild volume overload from acute on chronic 
systolic CHF (although CXR without evidence of edema and BNP 
less elevated than normal, pulmonary crackles) and bronchitis 
(productive cough of green-brown sputum). Transient nature of 
symptoms is reassuring, and he is being discharged without 
change in his home Furosemide dose.  Given minimal worsening of 
his renal function, we held his Lisinopril, and ordered him to 
have outpatient lab work done and faxed to Dr. ___ decision 
can be made whether to restart this as outpatient.
.  
On occasions he was somnolent during the day, but easily to 
arouse. This is felt to be due to his antidepressant. Dose was 
confirmed (Imipramine 125 mg), which is on to higher end of 
normal range for his age. We called his outpatient psychiatric 
provider, and left message with this regard. We recommended to 
patient and to patients healthcare proxy to arrange for follow 
up appointment with his psychiatrist to discuss his daytime 
sleepiness. 
.  
With regard to acute on chronic renal insufficiency: admitted 
with creatinine of 1.9 from recent baseline of 1.4-1.6. Improved 
through the course. Lisinopril is being held. Patient will have 
follow up appointment to reevaluate renal function and to 
consider restarting Lisinopril if renal function returned to 
baseline.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital after an episode of shortness 
of breath, fatigue and leg weakness.  Your chest x-ray showed 
that you were slightly volume overloaded, likely from your heart 
failure.  You received a dose of intravenous lasix and your 
symptoms improved.  Your kidney function was found to be 
slightly worse than usual.  We stopped your lisinopril, a drug 
that can cause kidney injury.  You need to have your blood work 
checked in one week so your physician can decide whether you 
should restart this medication.
Weigh yourself every morning, call MD if weight goes up more 
than 3 lbs.

care physician.

prescribed.

onset of dyspnea.  Evaluate for volume overload or infiltrate.

PA AND LATERAL CHEST RADIOGRAPH.

COMPARISON:  Chest radiograph, ___.

FINDINGS:  Single-lead AICD with the generator pack in the left upper chest is
stable.  There is moderate cardiomegaly, unchanged.  Lung volumes are slightly
low with slight bibasilar atelectasis.  Again noted is diffuse interestitial
markings most prominent in the lung bases.  No pleural effusions are noted. 
No pneumothorax is present.

IMPRESSION:  Mild pulmonary edema, likely cardiogenic.  Cardiomegaly with
atelectasis.  Otherwise, stable chest radiograph.
